Aomori|Japan.f: Aomori means green forest, a name likely taken from a small wooded hill that fishermen used as a landmark.

Okayama|Japan.f: Okayama is the setting of the Momotaro folk tale and home to Korakuen, ranked among Japan's top three traditional gardens.

Ibaraki|Japan.f: In 1976 a US C-5 hauled a defector's MiG-25 to Hyakuri Air Base, now Ibaraki Airport, where it was dismantled and studied.

Kitakyushu|Japan.f: Kitakyushu was created in 1963 by merging five cities and was the first designated city outside the Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya areas.

Niigata|Japan.f: After absorbing neighbors in 2005, Niigata gained more rice paddy acreage than any other city in Japan.

Shizuoka|Japan.f: After merging with Shimizu in 2003, Shizuoka briefly became the largest city by area in Japan, until Takayama overtook it in 2005.

Saga|Japan.f: Every autumn Saga holds its International Balloon Fiesta on the dry riverbed of the Kase River.

Tokushima|Japan.f: Tokushima grew rich in the Edo period as a distribution center for indigo and timber, and its merchants' wealth later seeded local banks.

Misawa|Japan.f: In 1931 the Miss Veedol took off from Misawa's Sabishiro Beach on the first nonstop flight across the Pacific, landing in Washington state.

Obihiro|Japan.f: Obihiro's Satsunai River, whose Ainu name means dry river, has been ranked Japan's cleanest Class A river seven times since 1991.

Kushiro|Japan.f: In 1945 the Soviets reportedly favoured Kushiro and Rumoi as the end points of a line splitting occupied Hokkaido.

Memanbetsu|Japan.f: Memanbetsu's name comes from the Ainu Memanpet, meaning river with a spring.

Yonago|Japan.f: In December 1950 US B-26 bombers moved to Miho Air Base near Yonago, then left for combat in the Korean War in May 1951.

Fukushima|Japan.f: Fukushima means lucky island, a name given to the local castle in the 1590s in imitation of the cheerful rename of Wakamatsu Castle.

Hanamaki|Japan.f: Hanamaki is the birthplace of poet and author Kenji Miyazawa and the home of Iwate's wanko soba, served in endless small bowls.

Ube|Japan.f: A great white pelican named Katta-kun, hatched in an Ube park in 1985, became famous for visiting local schools.

Asahikawa|Japan.f: Asahikawa recorded -41 C on January 25, 1902, the lowest temperature in Japanese history outside Mount Fuji.

Akita|Japan.f: At Akita's Kanto Festival, performers balance 15-meter bamboo poles hung with 230 lanterns on their chins.

Iwakuni|Japan.f: Iwakuni is home to gentle ivory-white snakes with ruby-red eyes, found in any concentration only there.

Hachijojima|Japan.f: Hachijo-jima was an Edo-period place of exile, and its own Hachijo language is on UNESCO's list of endangered languages.

Monbetsu|Japan.f: Monbetsu has made drift ice its symbol, with a sea ice museum and an international sea ice conference each February.

Toyama|Japan.f: Thanks to coastal shipping routes, Toyama became known across Japan as the province of medicine.

Wajima|Japan.f: Villagers of Nafune in Wajima say their gojinjo-daiko drumming began in 1577, when drums and devil masks scared off Uesugi Kenshin.

Izumo|Japan.f: A record from around 950 describes Izumo-taisha shrine as about 48 meters tall, higher than the 45-meter Todai-ji hall.

Tottori|Japan.f: Tottori has the smallest population of any prefectural capital in Japan, but its sand dunes host a university arid land research center.

Masuda|Japan.f: The painter Sesshu spent his last years in Masuda and died there in 1506 at age 87, and he designed gardens at two local temples.

Odate|Japan.f: Hachiko, the famously loyal Akita dog, came from Odate, where a visitor center now commemorates him.

Kumejima|Japan.f: Kumejima's deep seawater gives it Japan's largest market share of sea grapes and kuruma prawns.

Fukue|Japan.f: Fukue is the largest and southernmost of the Goto Islands, where 16th-century missionaries converted most of the population to Christianity.

Tokunoshima|Japan.f: Tokunoshima has the highest fertility rate in Japan and many supercentenarians, and its culture revolves around bull-versus-bull fights.

Matsumoto|Japan.f: Matsumoto's Kaichi School was one of the first modern schools built in Japan and is now a museum.

Shirahama|Japan.f: Shirahama means white beach, but development accelerated erosion and its famous white quartz sand began washing out to sea.

Nakashibetsu|Japan.f: Nakashibetsu is home to the easternmost airport on mainland Japan.

Wakkanai|Japan.f: Wakkanai holds Cape Soya, Japan's northernmost point, just 43 kilometers across the strait from Russia's Sakhalin Island.

Amami|Japan.f: Authorities fully eradicated the mongooses of Amami Oshima, whose numbers had reached 10,000 by 2000, by 2024.

Yamagata|Japan.f: Each September Yamagata serves thousands of bowls of imoni stew from a giant iron pot tended by a building crane.

Tsuruoka|Japan.f: Tsuruoka became Japan's 100th city in 1924 and is now the largest city in the Tohoku region by land area.

Miyakojima|Japan.f: Miyakojima's Irabu Ohashi Bridge, opened in 2015 and 3,540 meters long, is the longest toll-free bridge in Japan.

Tanegashima|Japan.f: Firearms were long called tanegashima in Japan after the island where Portuguese traders first introduced them.

Oki|Japan.f: The Oki Islands were a place of political exile, where Emperor Go-Toba died in 1221 and Emperor Go-Daigo escaped in 1332.
